Enhypostasia
en-hai-poh-STAY-zhuh
noun (Christology)
From Greek en (in) + hypostasis (person). The Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is personalized in (enhypostatized by) the divine Person. Paired with anhypostasia (the human nature has no independent personhood of its own).

📖 Biblical Definition

From Greek en (in) + hypostasis (person, subsistence); the Christological doctrine that the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is personalized in (enhypostatized by) the divine Person of the Word. The doctrine, developed principally by Leontius of Byzantium (6th century) and refined in subsequent Christology, addresses a precise question raised by the two-natures doctrine: in what person does the human nature of Christ subsist? The answer is paired in two terms. Anhypostasia (from an-, without, + hypostasis): the human nature of Christ has no independent personhood of its own — it never existed as a separate human person; there is no human person of Jesus alongside the divine Person. Enhypostasia (from en-, in): the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — the human nature is real and complete (a true human nature, body and reasonable soul) but is personalized in the divine Person, never having a separate personhood. The two terms together express the orthodox doctrine: the human nature of Christ is complete but not independently personal; it subsists in and is personalized by the Person of the Word; there are not two persons (against Nestorianism) but one Person (the eternal Son) subsisting in two natures, the human nature being enhypostatic (personalized in the divine Person). This guards against two errors: Nestorianism (which would make the human nature an independent person, producing two persons in Christ) and the supposition that the human nature is impersonal in the sense of being incomplete or sub-human. The human nature is fully and completely human (lacking nothing proper to humanity except sin) but is personalized in the divine Person of the Son rather than constituting a separate human person. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine of enhypostasia (with anhypostasia): the human nature of Christ is real, complete, and personalized in the Person of the eternal Son; there is one Person (the Word) subsisting in two natures, the human nature having its personal subsistence in the divine Person; this preserves the unity of Christ's Person (against Nestorianism) and the completeness of His human nature (against the incompleteness errors).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

From Greek en (in) + hypostasis (person); the doctrine that the human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son (personalized in the divine Person); paired with anhypostasia (the human nature has no independent personhood); developed by Leontius of Byzantium; guards the unity of Christ's Person against Nestorianism.

ENHYPOSTASIA, n. (Christology; Greek en [in] + hypostasis [person]) The human nature of Christ has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son — personalized in (enhypostatized by) the divine Person of the Word. Developed by Leontius of Byzantium (6th c.). Paired with anhypostasia (the human nature has no independent personhood of its own; it never existed as a separate human person). Together: the human nature is real and complete (true body and reasonable soul) but is personalized in the divine Person, never having a separate personhood. Guards against Nestorianism (two persons) and against treating the human nature as incomplete. One Person (the Word) in two natures, the human nature enhypostatic (personalized in the divine Person).

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."

Hebrews 2:14 — "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same."

Hebrews 2:16-17 — "For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren."

Philippians 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Enhypostasia (with anhypostasia) guards the unity of Christ's Person and the completeness of His human nature; it is held against Nestorianism (making the human nature an independent person, producing two persons) and the incompleteness errors.

Enhypostasia (with its paired term anhypostasia) is a precise Christological doctrine that guards the unity of Christ's Person and the completeness of His human nature. The doctrine addresses a question raised by the two-natures Christology: in what person does the human nature of Christ subsist? The answer guards against two errors. Nestorianism would make the human nature an independent human person, producing two persons in Christ (the divine person of the Word and a separate human person of Jesus, united only morally); this contradicts the unity of Christ's Person (Christ is one Person, not two). The incompleteness errors would suppose that, because the human nature has no independent personhood, it is somehow incomplete or sub-human; this contradicts the completeness of Christ's human nature (He was made like His brethren in all things, Hebrews 2:17, lacking nothing proper to humanity except sin). The doctrine of enhypostasia-with-anhypostasia holds the substantive balance: the human nature of Christ is real and complete (a true human nature, body and reasonable soul) but never existed as an independent human person (anhypostasia); rather, it has its personal subsistence in the Person of the eternal Son (enhypostasia), personalized in the divine Person. There is one Person (the Word) subsisting in two natures; the human nature is enhypostatic, personalized in the divine Person, never constituting a separate human person. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive doctrine: the human nature of Christ is real, complete, and personalized in the Person of the eternal Son; this preserves the unity of Christ's Person (against Nestorianism) and the completeness of His humanity, undergirding the two-natures Christology of Chalcedon.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek en + hypostasis; the human nature personalized in the Person of the eternal Son; paired with anhypostasia (no independent personhood); Leontius of Byzantium; guards the unity of Christ's Person against Nestorianism.
